title: Cert Authorities Check for DNSSEC from Today
text: > The TL;DR is that by the time DANE was created the WebPKI already existed and was universal and so adding DANE didn't buy you anything because you still were going to have to have a WebPKI certificate more or less in perpetuity. Yet somehow they managed to wrangle hundreds of CAs to use the CT logs and to change the mandated set of algorithms. > Well, back when people were taking DNSSEC and DANE more seriously, there was a lot of talk of doing DNSSEC Transparency. And this would have been great. But it only needs to make transparent the changes in delegation (actually, only DS records) from the TLD to my zone. Not anything _within_ my zone. And tellingly, the efforts to enable delegation in WebPKI are going nowhere. Even though X.509 is supporting it from the beginning (via name constraints, a critical extension). > This is hyperbole, because nobody is forcing you to update the TLS cert every 7 days. The eventual plan is to have shorter certs. 47 days will be mandated by 2029. It also doesn't really change my point: I can't have a purely static server anymore and expect it to be accessible. > Moreover, the same basic situation applies to DNSSEC, because your zone also needs to be signed frequently, for the same underlying reason: disabling compromised or mississued credentials. That's incorrect. I've been using the same key (inside my HSM) since 2016. And I don't have to update the zone if it's unchanged. DNSSEC is actually _more_ secure than TLS, because zone signing can be done fully offline. With TLS, the key material is often a buggy memcpy() away from the corrosive anonymous Internet environment. So you can rotate the DNSSEC keys, but it's neither mandated nor necessary. The need for short-lived certs for TLS is because there's no way to check their validity online during the request (OCSP is dead and CRLs are too bulky). But with DNSSEC if at any point my signing key is compromised, I can just change the DS records in the registrar to point to my updated key.

title: WebPKI and You
text: > browsers can and do set their own rules. Here's a link to the minutes of the CABF meeting where the 25 certificate issuers and the 4 browser vendors—Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla—agreed to reduce the validity period of TLS certificates unanimously [1]. > The reduction of TLS cert lifetime to a max of 398 days was an Apple policy. Actually, all of the browser vendors voted to reduce the validity period of TLS certificates from 825 days to 398 days at the September 2019 meeting. The ballot failed because a majority of the certificate issuers voted against it. At the February 2020 CABF meeting, Apple announced it would unilaterally enforce the 398-day limit through its own root program policy. Starting September 1, 2020, any new TLS certificate with a validity period exceeding 398 days would simply not be trusted by Safari, macOS, or iOS. text: Honest reply: because the infrastructure isn't ready to support 1-day certificates yet. If your cert is only valid for one day, and renewal fails on a Saturday, then your site is unusable until you get back to work on Monday and do something to fix it. There are things that can be done to mitigate this risk, like using an ACME client which supports fallback between multiple CAs, but the vast majority of sites out there today simply aren't set up to handle that yet. The point of the CA/BF settling on 47-day certs is yes, to strongly push automation, but also to still allow time for manual intervention when automation fails.

title: Upcoming Changes to Let's Encrypt Certificates
text: Tons of information for research, hackers, you name it ... It shows a history of domains, you can find hidden subdomains, still active, revoked etc ... The main issue is that currently you can not easily revoke certs, so your almost forced to keep a history of certs, and when one has been revoked in the CT logs. In theory, if everybody is forced to change certs every 47 days, sure, you can invalidated them and permanently remove them. But it requires a ton of automatization on the user side. There is still way too much software that relies on a single year or multi year certificated that is manually added to it. Its also why the fadeout to 47 days, is over a 4 year time periode. And it still does not change the massive increased in requests to check validation, that hits CT logs providers.
author: benjiro

title: Upcoming Changes to Let's Encrypt Certificates
text: The certificate lifetime decrease, to 45 days, was discussed in: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=46117126 This isn't LE's decision: a 47 day max was voted on by the CA/Browser Forum. https://www.digicert.com/blog/tls-certificate-lifetimes-will... https://cabforum.org/2025/04/11/ballot-sc081v3-introduce-sch... https://groups.google.com/a/groups.cabforum.org/g/servercert... - public votes of all members, which were unanimously Yes or Abstain. IMO this is a policy change that can Break the Internet, as many archived/legacy sites on old-school certificates may not be able to afford the upfront tech or ongoing labor to transition from annual to effectively-monthly renewals, and will simply be shut down. And, per other comments, this will make LE the only viable option to modernize, and thus much more of a central point of failure than before. But Let's Encrypt is not responsible for this move, and did not vote on the ballot.

text: Well sure, that is the argument behind short-lived certs but the current standard (47 days or less) is still fairly long if you think about a targeted attack. If you use DANE this is already possible but quite fragile unless you have configured your TLS certificate issuing server to have access to modify your DNS records (which is probably less safe overall).
author: cyphar

title: OCSP Service Has Reached End of Life
text: > The underlying dynamics of any change to the Web ecosystem is that it has to be incrementally deployable, in the sense that when element A changes it doesn't experience breakage with the existing ecosystem. Absolutely, this is important. But I don't understand why this should have any effect on OCSP-stapling vs. CRL. As you note, "approximately no Web servers do OCSP stapling, so any browser which requires it will just not work." But browsers also cannot rely on CRLs being 100% available and up-to-date. Enforcing OCSP stapling and enforcing a check against an up-to-date CRL would both require this kind of incremental or iterative deployment. > As an aside it's not clear that OCSP stapling is better than short-lived certs. This is equally applicable to CRL, though. The current plan for phased reduction of TLS cert lifespan is to stabilize at 47 days in 2029. If reducing cert lifetime achieves the goal of reducing the value of compromised certs, then any mechanism for revoking/invalidating certificates will be reduced in value.
author: dlenski

title: OCSP Service Has Reached End of Life
text: OCSP stapling was a good solution in the age of certificates that were valid for 10 years (which was the case for basic HTTPS certificates back in 2011 when OCSP stapling was introduced). In the age of 90 day certificates (to be reduced to a maximum of 47 days in a few years), it's not quite as necessary any more, but I don't think OCSP stapling is that problematic a solution. Certificates in air-gapped networks are problematic, but that problem can be solved with dedicated CRL-only certificate roots that suffer all of the downsides of CRLs for cases where OCSP stapling isn't available. Nobody will miss OCSP now that it's dead, but assuming you used stapling I think it was a decent solution to a difficult problem that plagued the web for more than a decade and a half.

title: Stop SSL certificate outages with automated monitoring – Enterprise Ready
text: Totally fair, and for a single cert or a tightly controlled setup, a calendar reminder might be “enough.” But in practice, it tends to break down when: - Certificates multiply across internal services, vendors, CDNs, load balancers, staging/prod, and even IoT or embedded devices. Ownership is unclear, people leave, and calendar invites don’t update themselves. No visibility, unless someone’s checking regularly, you won’t know if a cert was rotated early, replaced with a shorter one, or removed entirely. No alerting or state tracking, a calendar doesn’t notify you if someone messed up the renewal or if the cert is already expired. No integration with the rest of your monitoring/incident tooling. SSL Guardian gives you a real-time dashboard of every cert, expiration tracking, and actual notifications, so you’re not relying on tribal knowledge, calendar hygiene, or someone noticing too late. We’re not trying to over-engineer a reminder, we’re replacing a fragile human process with something that scales across orgs and environments. title: Show HN: Never have an SSL certificate expire again
text: > Is expiration monitoring done solely through certificate transparency logs or also by connecting to the host? For every detected host, the app periodically performs an SSL handshake (HTTPS only), and checks for the expiration of the served cert. CT is used to detect new certs, and extract relevant hosts from these certs. > Can the service monitor hosts that aren't accessible publicly? Nope, this runs as a Heroku app right now, and will work with publicly accessible HTTPS-serving hosts only. > Does this service support certificate checking for certificates that aren't on certificate transparency logs? Yes, CT is used to detect new hosts automatically. The app also relies on the SANS of the certs it finds, spreading as wide as possible within the domain of interest. The actual checking of certs is a simple HTTPS handshake and inspection of the served cert.
author: adrukh

title: Letsencrypt, the Good, the Bad and the Ugly
text: > So it required less of my attention than before. And that is why we run it. But we still monitor. First we pipe stdout things to syslog via logger(1) to record each run in cron; however stderr is not redirected so we get that sent to us. Further, in our hook scripts, we have an "apache2ctl configtest" when a cert is renewed to verify that Apache (or equivalent) can read the files correctly, then we do the restart/reload. The configtest is sent to stderr as well so we can track when renewals happen and when there's an issue. On top of all that, we don't actually trust our ACME client(s) to work properly all the time, so we check the expiration time on our certificates. We're monitoring the HTTP(S) service anyway, so adding another check doesn't add much cost. And all this runs in the background silently and it only becomes top-of-mind really when it shows up in our service alert dashboard.

title: New TLS certificate for .herokuapp.com hostnames
text: We run a backend API app on Heroku and for simplicity our frontend calls it via the herokuapp.com subdomain `<our-app-name>.herokuapp.com`. We haven't bothered with a custom domain SSL certificate as the herokuapp.com subdomain has been just fine. Fortunately I was monitoring the endpoint as I started getting SSL expiry warnings a few weeks ago. It seems heroku is serving an old certificate for <our-app-name>.herokuapp.com, issued April 2019 and expiring 22nd June: ``` $ curl -v --head https://<our-app-name>.herokuapp.com/ * Connected to <our-app-name>.herokuapp.com (52.19.225.66) port 443 (#0) [snip] * Server certificate: * expire date: Jun 22 12:00:00 2020 GMT * subjectAltName: host "<our-app-name>.herokuapp.com" matched cert's " .herokuapp.com" issuer: C=US; O=DigiCert Inc; OU=www.digicert.com; CN=DigiCert SHA2 High Assurance Server CA ``` It's a wildcard cert for .herokuapp.com but it's different from the current one I see if I curl the root domain: ``` $ curl -v --head https://herokuapp.com/ Connected to herokuapp.com (34.194.84.166) port 443 (#0) * Server certificate: * expire date: Aug 2 02:13:11 2020 GMT * issuer: C=US; O=Let's Encrypt; CN=Let's Encrypt Authority X3 ``` It seems they've transitioned to Let's Encrypt for the wildcard domain, but it isn't being served for app subdomains. I've checked a few other subdomains and see the same thing: * govuk-prototype-kit.herokuapp.com * heroku-status.herouapp.com * juice-shop.herokuapp.com I've been raising this with support since T-30 and they just keep saying things like: > Our concerned team is aware of it and they are actively working on the renewal process. We'll get the new cert in there well before the expiration, and there will be no disruption of service. Now we're at 7 days I've lost confidence that support has even forwarded my ticket to the right team. I suspect in 7 days we're gonna see a lot of things break...
author: paulfurley

title: LetsEncrypt – Expiration Notification Service Has Ended
text: This is a smart move. The amount of infrastructure complexity for what's essentially a band-aid for poor automation practices wasn't worth it. We migrated ~800 domains to LE back in 2019 and initially relied heavily on those expiration emails as a safety net. But honestly, they became more of a crutch than a help. Once we implemented proper monitoring with Prometheus + cert-manager, we haven't had a single cert expire unexpectedly. The privacy angle is interesting too. I hadn't considered how much PII they were sitting on just for this feature. With GDPR and similar regulations, that's a significant liability for what amounts to "your cron job didn't run" notifications. For anyone panicking about this: if you're still depending on email notifications for cert renewal in 2025, this is your wake-up call to implement actual monitoring. Even a simple bash script that checks cert expiry dates and posts to a Slack webhook would be more reliable than email notifications. Curious what their infrastructure costs actually were for this. "Tens of thousands per year" seems low for managing millions of emails, but I guess if it's just queuing jobs to an email service provider, that tracks.
author: builtsimple

title: Ask HN: Any good "cert expired" horror stories?
text: Most places I have worked had Nagios or other monitoring in place for the certs but there is always some end point that nobody in operations new about. The most common were things added by marketing outside of normal change control. Those were self induced horror stories for the marketing team I suppose. I this case if you had a tool I think your best bet would be to partner with all the CMS providers that marketing teams or any team that tends to skip change control tend to use and make it a value added service. I've also seen some certs expired for obscure government endpoints used to validate information about people. The most challenging part of that was not technical but rather finding someone that could fix it and cared enough to treat it with any level of urgency. The only option to monitor those was internal monitoring tools as they are in most cases firewall restricted meaning any tool someone makes would have to be self hosted. We would notify them ahead of time. Then notify them again. Then try to call someone. The bigger challenge with these was not expiration but rather chain validation when they would not install intermediate certs and then expect us to install of their certs on our tens of thousands of servers as a work around. Nobody would believe me if I said which agency had this problem the most often but this will be our little secret .
author: LinuxBender

title: Single dependency stacks
text: I'm not sure what qualifies as "stateful", but > Fewer dependencies to fail and take down the service. No logging? No metrics? No monitoring? (& yes , you'd think those shouldn't take down the stack if they went offline. And I'd agree. And yet, I've witnessed that failure mode multiple times. In one, a call to Sentry was synchronous & a hard-fail, so when Sentry went down, that service 500'd. In another, syslog couldn't push logs out to the logging service, as that was very down, having been inadvertently deleted by someone who ran "terraform apply", didn't read the plan, & then said "make it so"; syslog then responded to the logging service being down by logging that error to a local file. Repeatedly. As fast as it possibly could. Fill the disk. Disk is full. Service fails.) I've also seen our alerting provider have an outage during an outage we're having & thus not sending pages for our outage, causing me to ponder and wonder how I'd just rolled a 1 on the SRE d20 and what god did I anger? Also who watches the watchmen? > A common pitfall is to introduce something like ElasticSearch, only to realize a few months later that no one knows how to run it. Yeah I've seen that exact pit fallen into. No DNS? Global Cloudflare outage == fun. No certificates? I've seen certs fail so many different way. Of course not getting renewed, that's your table stakes "welcome to certs!" failure mode. Certs get renewed but an allegedly Semver compatible upgrade changed the defaults, and required extensions don't get included leading to the client rejecting the cert. I've seen a service which watches certs to make sure they don't expire (see the outage earlier in this paragraph!) have an outage (which, b/c it's monitoring, wasn't customer visible) because a tool issued a malformed cert (…by… default…) that the monitor failed to parse (as it was malformed). Oh, and then the LE cross-signing expiration took out an Azure service that wasn't ready for it, a service from a third-party of ours that wasn't ready for it, and our CI system b/c several tools were out of date including an up to date system on Debian that was theoretically "supported"… but still shipped an ancient crypto library riddled with bugs in its path validation. > Okay fine, S3 too, but that’s a different animal. Is it? I've seen that have outages too, & bring down a service with it. (There really wasn't a choice there; S3 was the service's backing store, & without it, the service was truly screwed.) But of course, all this is to say I violently agree with the article's core point: think carefully about each dependency, as they have a very real production cost. (I've recently been considering changing my title to SRE because I have done very little in the way of SWE recently…)

title: Support for shortlived certificates
text: ### 📑 I have found these related issues/pull requests https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma/issues/6779 ### 🔖 Feature description Currently, Uptime Kuma treats TLS certificates with very short validity periods as expiring, which triggers warnings and notifications even though the certificates are still valid by design. However, the EFF has recently announced official support for short-lived TLS certificates with a lifetime of just six days. These certificates are intended to improve security by significantly reducing the impact window of key compromise and encouraging automated, continuous renewal workflows. I know, you can already set when notifications are being sent. But the system isn't generally ready for short-lived certificates yet. ### ✔️ Solution As short-lived certificates gain broader adoption, monitoring systems like Uptime Kuma may need to adapt their expiration logic to distinguish between genuinely expiring certificates and intentionally short-lived ones that are regularly rotated. ### ❓ Alternatives _No response_ ### 📝 Additional Context _No response_

title: Allow for different cert expiration intervals to be able to handle shorter lifetime certificates
text: ### 📑 I have found these related issues/pull requests Various ones related, but not seeing any specifically regarding configuring different intervals based on the cert total lifetime. ### 🔖 Feature description Allow configuring the expiration warnings either A) based on percentage of life or B) different set of options for shorter lifetimes. Everyone should be used to 90d certs now with LE, but various providers are moving along with offering shorter lifetimes - 30d is pretty commonly available to future proof for the eventual 45 day requirement, but also LE has the 7d certs. When you have a mix of 'max lifetime 200d' and 'short 30d/7d' certs, it's hard to have a reasonable setting. ### ✔️ Solution Simplest implementation would just be to allow the configuration to be based on percent-of-life instead of fixed days, but it would be nice to have a bit more tuning. i.e. allow "days" and "percent" as suffixes in the dropdown. 7d certs for example I don't need to get an alert unless they have 2d left in most cases, but for a long life cert that I probably had to jump through hoops for, I sure don't want to wait till 2d left. Configuring alert for "< 30% of lifetime" is going to be a good alerting setting for any certificate that you have automated replacement for on pretty much any of the endpoints. ### ❓ Alternatives Allow the 'TLS Cert Expiry' configuration to be overriden on a per monitor basis. That would also couple in nicely with a bunch of other feature request issues I saw asking for different types/ports/etc. of x509/cert monitoring. ### 📝 Additional Context _No response_

text: ### 📑 I have found these related issues/pull requests - #5083 — This issue asks a very similar question: whether Uptime Kuma can monitor only the certificate expiration time without monitoring the website/service itself. My request is essentially the same use case, but I would like to propose it as a dedicated monitor/check type for HTTP(S)/TLS certificates. - #5358 — This issue focuses on improving certificate expiry notifications, variables, and configurable alert thresholds. It is related, but it still assumes certificate monitoring as part of existing HTTPS monitors. - #5609 — This issue asks for a certificate-expiration-only dashboard. It is related from a UI/reporting perspective, but this request is specifically about having an actual monitor type/check that only evaluates the certificate. - #1079 — This requests SSL certificate checks for general TCP ports. It is related because it expands certificate monitoring beyond classic HTTPS checks, but my request focuses on HTTP(S)/TLS certificate expiry without considering the HTTP service status as the primary check. - #844 / #3229 / #5374 — These are related to configuring certificate expiry checks and alert behavior, but they do not provide a certificate-only monitor. ### 🔖 Feature description Uptime Kuma already supports certificate expiry notifications for HTTP(S) monitors. However, this is currently tied to monitoring the service/website itself. It would be very useful to have a dedicated monitor type or option that checks only the TLS/SSL certificate expiration of a given host, without treating the HTTP service availability, HTTP status code, response body, keyword checks, redirects, or general uptime of the website as the main monitoring target. Use case: I want to monitor customer certificates and notify customers before their certificates expire. In this case, I do not necessarily want to monitor whether the customer’s website or service is currently up or down. I only want to track the certificate

title: Clarify domain expiry warning for unsupported TLDs yet more
text: ### 📑 I have found these related issues/pull requests #6620 already has improved this, but considering several issues about unsupported TLDs have appeared since, further improvement may make sense. ### 🔖 Feature description Since #6620, the log entry for when a domain's TLD is not supported for its expiration date to be checked is defined as follows: ``` log.warn("domain", `Domain expiry unsupported for '.${tld.publicSuffix}' because its RDAP endpoint is not listed in the IANA database.`); ``` ### ✔️ Solution I would propose adding an explanation that helps users to understand the issue better. My idea: ``` log.warn("domain", `Domain expiry unsupported for the TLD '.${tld.publicSuffix}' because it has no RDAP endpoint in the IANA database. The TLD's registry presumably has no official RDAP endpoint at all and may be not publishing any expiration dates in general.`); ``` ### ❓ Alternatives _No response_ ### 📝 Additional Context The trouble with the current message is: The user may think that `.de` or `.eu` being amongst the most popular TLDs in the whole internet, they must support RDAP, don't they? Actually, they don't. Just because a TLD is popular doesn't mean it supports RDAP. And this is why I propose adding an explanation to the message, because a. DENIC and EURid probably don't support RDAP (yet) because they publish limited data in general because of EU GDPR, and b. DENIC and EURid don't publish expiration dates at all. For those not in the know, DENIC is the registry behind `.de` and EURid the registry for `.eu`. If anyone else has better ideas of how to phrase it, feel free to add your proposal.

title: `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` errors
text: ### 📑 I have found these related issues/pull requests * #1957 - introduced a `busy_timeout` * bc86f8b - reverted it again * #6979 - the presumed cause for my issue * #7095, #6486, #7260 might be related, sometimes in part, although the reported error message isn't always the exact same. ### 🛡️ Security Policy - [x] I have read and agree to Uptime Kuma's [Security Policy](https://github.com/louislam/uptime-kuma/security/policy). ### 📝 Description After upgrading to 2.2.0, I keep seeing regular (sometimes daily) `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` errors in the error log. The log does not show errors before the release of 2.2.0. I suspect this is a consequence/regression from #6979 , probably because I am running uptime kuma on a Raspberry Pi with an SD card. I noticed that #1957 introduced a `busy_timeout` but it was reverted in bc86f8b (without further context). As far as I know, the default is 0, meaning it fails immediately when a lock is held. On an SD card, this could be an issue with concurrent writes on a slower medium. My instance isn't very big, I have 13 Monitors, most are HTTPS, some TCP. The errors seem to appear mostly around times when scheduled tasks are running, such as a nightly backup script (in my case at 01:30). Would you be open to reintroducing `busy_timeout` or a config paramter to allow manually setting the connection pool size? ### 👟 Reproduction steps 1. Run Uptime Kuma 2.2.0 or later on a Raspberry Pi with an SD card as storage medium 2. Configure a dozen HTTP(S) monitors with 60s interval 3. Add scheduled tasks that involve reading/writing to the SD card (concurrent disk I/O) 4. Check error.log in the data directory ### 👀 Expected behavior No `SQLITE_BUSY` errors in error.log, as was the case before 2.2.0. ### 😓 Actual Behavior `SQLITE_BUSY: database is locked` errors appear regularly in error.log, affecting `stat_minutely`, `stat_hourly`, `stat_daily`, `heartbeat`, and `monitor_tls_info` tables. title: [Bug]: Documentation describes expiration emails that may not be sent
text: ### Certbot Version 4.1.1 ### What happened? Looking at the documentation user guide: https://eff-certbot.readthedocs.io/en/stable/using.html It has a couple sentences that are misleading: > Generally, there’s no need to revoke a certificate if its private key has not been compromised, but you may still receive expiration emails from Let’s Encrypt unless you revoke. and > Please note that the CA will send notification emails to the address you provide if you do not renew certificates that are about to expire. [Let's Encrypt no longer provides expiration emails](https://letsencrypt.org/2025/01/22/ending-expiration-emails/), (and other CAs can of course also be used with certbot), so these sentences should be updated. ### Expected behavior I would expect something along the lines of > Generally, there’s no need to revoke a certificate if its private key has not been compromised, and one can just let it expire at its normal expiration time. and > Please note that some CAs may send notification emails to the address you provide if you do not renew certificates that are about to expire, or you may want to utilize other monitoring tools to ensure that your certificates are renewed as expected. Though I'm sure better wordings are possible.

author: Ezwen

title: Undocumented systemd magic breaks certain renewal workflows
text: On Ubuntu 16.04+, certbot automatically runs a renewal command twice a day via a systemd timer. This magic feature is totally undocumented. Furthermore, the documentation on cert renewal (https://certbot.eff.org/docs/using.html#renewing-certificates) suggests that the user should set up their own renewal command, and place it in a crontab. The user's renewal command may include custom options, such as renewal/deployment hooks. However, the default renewal command in the systemd service may preempt the user's renewal command, renew the certificate, and completely bypass the user's custom renewal/deployment hooks. Rough example of how to reproduce: Register and request the initial cert, using the procedure at https://certbot.eff.org/docs/using.html#manual ```sh certbot register --non-interactive --agree-tos --email 'admin@email.com.example' --no-eff-email certbot certonly --manual --non-interactive --manual-public-ip-logging-ok \ --domains "domain.com.example" \ --preferred-challenges dns \ --manual-auth-hook /opt/my_certbot_hooks/auth_hook.sh \ --manual-cleanup-hook /opt/my_certbot_hooks/cleanup_hook.sh ``` Deploy the cert (deployment commands do not matter). Then, make a crontab that runs the following command once a week: ```sh certbot renew --non-interactive \ --renew-hook "/opt/my_certbot_hooks/renew_hook.sh" ``` When the cert nears expiration, it is likely that the systemd service will run first and renew it. As a result, our renewal command will be a no-op and `renew_hook.sh` will never be called.

author: basd82

title: --dry-run and expiration e-mails
text: Running Certbot with `--dry-run` can cause expiration e-mails from staging. How? 1. If you do not yet have a staging account and you've provided an e-mail address on the command line or in a configuration file, Certbot will use that e-mail address when creating a new account, resulting in expiration e-mails from staging. 2. If you already have a staging account, Certbot uses it. If this staging account has an e-mail address registered to it, you will receive expiration e-mails (unless you've unsubscribed). We should fix this, first by never using an e-mail address with `--dry-run` and second by always creating a new, temporary staging account, which is not saved to disk.
author: bmw

title: --auto-hsts should disable HSTS if renewal has failed N times
text: Having an HSTS header makes a certificate error unrecoverable on the user end, which is obviously very bad. The `--auto-hsts` option should try to avoid contributing to such situations if at all possible. It's reasonably common for certificate renewal to be failing for some silly reason, but if that's happening the auto hsts code should notice and disable the HSTS header to mitigate the damage. Ideally there should be a constraint `N + HSTS-max-age-in-days < 30`, if that's possible.

title: renewal notice : email should sequence the domain names correctly
text: #### Background Suppose a certificate was created using a command of the form > letsencrypt-auto run -d www.example.com -d example.com .... Note the order in which the domain names appear. #### Observed behavior The renewal email mentions the relevant domain names in some wacky order: > example.com, www.example.com #### Desired behavior - It should mention them in the correct order ... at least with the correct name first. This is important, because the certificate files are named after the **first** domain name mentioned on the command line, as discussed in item #1376. - The email should be even more explicit: It should say like: > To renew the same set of domain names, pass the following options on the command line: > -d www.example.com -d example.com
author: JohnDenker

title: Client should strongly encourage use of an email address
text: If the CA has many (/any) users with no email on file, it's going to cause a lot of hassles. We're still deciding if we want it to be official policy that everyone has to provide an email, but in the meantime we can work on the client side of this. Proposal: The interactive version of the client should ask for an email, and not proceed without one, unless it was invoked with a --allow-unsafe-registration. The help documentation for --allow-unsafe-registration would say: "Specifying this flag enables registering an account with no email address. This is strongly discouraged, because in the event of key loss or account compromise you will irrevocably lose access to your account. You will also be unable to receive notice about impending expiration of revocation of your certificates. Updates to the Subscriber Agreement will still affect you, and the CA will make a best-effort attempt to notify you about them based on information about the affected domains, such as WHOIS data and common administrative addresses."
author: jsha

title: Portal never renews an expired client certificate; rotation requires manual revoke
text: ## Problem When a client certificate expires, the user is locked out of the VPN. They can't get a working profile back through the portal by themselves. The server rejects the expired certificate during the TLS handshake: ``` VERIFY OK: depth=1, ... CN= VERIFY ERROR: depth=0, error=certificate has expired: ... CN=user@example.com Sent fatal SSL alert: certificate expired TLS Error: TLS handshake failed ``` Signing in to the portal and downloading the profile again returns **the same expired certificate**. The only way to get a new one is for an operator to revoke the old certificate on the server: ``` ih-openvpn revoke-client user@example.com ``` After that, the next portal visit issues a new certificate. ## Root cause `ensure_certificate()` in `portal/portal/__init__.py` only checks whether the certificate file exists: ```python def ensure_certificate(config_dir, email): cert_path = osp.join(config_dir, "pki", "issued", f"{email}.crt") if not osp.exists(cert_path): generate_client_key(config_dir, email) ``` It never looks at the certificate's validity. `/profile` packages whatever is in `pki/issued/ .crt`, so an expired certificate gets served again indefinitely. Client certificates are signed with Easy-RSA's default lifetime (`EASYRSA_CERT_EXPIRE`, 825 days). That means every user onboarded around the same time hits this within days of each other, about 2 years 3 months after the initial rollout. ## Expected behavior Rotating a certificate should be self-service and shouldn't need an operator. When an expired or nearly expired certificate is renewed, the old one should also be revoked, so it can't be used anywhere else. ## Proposed changes 1. **Renew automatically in the portal.** In `ensure_certificate()`, read the certificate's `notAfter`. If the certificate is expired or inside a renewal window, revoke the old certificate, regenerate the CRL, and issue a new key and certificate. Do this under a lock so concurrent re

text: ### Goal Know that production is down, full or failing before a user says so. ### Work - [ ] External uptime check on `https://dixpertia.tn/api/health` and `https://dixpertia.com` (e.g. Uptime Kuma, or a free external service), alerting by e-mail. - [ ] Alerts for disk over 80%, memory pressure, a failed backup (#171) and a failed deploy. - [ ] TLS certificate expiry alert, in case Let's Encrypt renewal fails. - [ ] Logs: - API and Traefik logs kept and searchable in Dokploy for the retention period; - no secrets or passwords in them (already the rule in the code); - IP addresses only as long as the retention policy allows. - [ ] Alerts on security signals: repeated 429s from #175, bursts of 401s, or a spike in 5xx errors. - [ ] A short "what to do when" page in the runbook: site down, disk full, database down, certificate expired. ### Related #183, #184, #171, #175, #187.

title: Design public TLS ingress and certificate renewal

title: Distinguish SSL/certificate errors from other connection errors
text: ## What happens When the NAS certificate is expired or untrusted, or the TLS handshake fails, the library raises a generic `SynologyDSMRequestException`. For an expired certificate the message only contains the aiohttp `ConnectionKey`: ClientConnectorCertificateError = ConnectionKey(host='nas.local', port=5001, ...) The actual reason ("certificate has expired") is lost, and consumers can't distinguish a certificate problem from other connection errors (host down, wrong port, timeout) to give the user a useful message. The last renewal of my SSL cert failed due to a recent DSM 7.4 requirements, suddenly Home Assistant Synology integration showed an error. Because the error had nothing to do with my SSL cert, I wasn't sure of the issue and ... sadly, never had time to investigate. Yesterday I realized my SSL was expired and after renewed it, HA stopped to complain. ## Expected A dedicated exception for SSL/TLS errors that still subclasses `SynologyDSMRequestException` (so existing handlers keep working), with the actual reason in the details. ## Proposal Add `SynologyDSMSSLException(SynologyDSMRequestException)`, raised for `ClientConnectorCertificateError`, `ClientSSLError` and `ssl.SSLError` in `_execute_request`, and use it in the Home Assistant integration to show a proper message. I can open a PR if you agree with the approach. I also plan to create a PR for HA integration so the error shows up properly to the enduser. Before proceeded, I'll wait to see if any comments are added in here. Thanx!

title: Expired TLS certificate on annotationapi.pyronear.org
text: This issue is part of the epic pyronear/roadmap#21 (Annotation tool quality). ## Summary The production annotation API endpoint `https://annotationapi.pyronear.org` is serving an **expired Let's Encrypt certificate**, breaking all TLS-verifying clients. ## Evidence ``` $ echo | openssl s_client -connect annotationapi.pyronear.org:443 -servername annotationapi.pyronear.org 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates subject=CN = annotationapi.pyronear.org issuer=C = US, O = Let's Encrypt, CN = R13 notBefore=Apr 9 13:15:55 2026 GMT notAfter =Jul 8 13:15:54 2026 GMT ``` The certificate expired on **2026-07-08** (~9 days ago as of 2026-07-17). ## Impact - Any HTTPS client that verifies certificates fails with `SSLError(SSLCertVerificationError: certificate has expired)`. - The data-transfer scripts that talk to the remote (`make pull-sequences`, `make pull-seq-annotations`, `make push-annotations`) cannot authenticate or connect. - The only current workaround is disabling TLS verification, which is insecure and should not be a standing practice. ## Reproduce ``` make pull-sequences MAX_SEQUENCES=5 READ_ONLY_SOURCE=1 # -> Source annotation auth failed: SSLError(... certificate has expired ...) ``` ## Suggested fix - Renew/redeploy the Let's Encrypt certificate on `annotationapi.pyronear.org` (the auto-renewal / certbot hook likely failed silently). - Add expiry monitoring/alerting so this is caught before expiration next time.
author: Chouffe

title: Signing profile certificate renewal contract
text: ### Description The full contract surface for renewing the certificate on a signing profile that uses the MANAGED / STATIC_KEY signing scheme, kept as one issue because the pieces are only useful together. In scope: - The renewal endpoint and its renewal-record DTOs, including the 404, 409 renewal-already-in-progress and 422 no-RA-profile responses. - Three resource events - `SIGNING_PROFILE_CERTIFICATE_RENEWAL_REQUESTED`, `_COMPLETED` and `_FAILED` - so renewal progress reaches the notification panel. - A `RENEW_SIGNING_PROFILE_CERTIFICATE` execution type, so renewal can be driven automatically from a trigger rule on `CERTIFICATE_EXPIRING`. - Certificate validity status on the signing profile list and detail DTOs, so the UI can show it without a second lookup per profile. The design this implements is on the [core] umbrella. ### User Story As a signing administrator, I can renew the certificate behind a signing profile through the API and be told how it went, so that a profile does not stop working because its certificate expired. ### Use Case Actor: a signing administrator, or the trigger engine acting automatically. Precondition: a MANAGED / STATIC_KEY profile whose certificate has an RA profile. Flow: the caller requests renewal and receives a renewal record reference; progress and outcome arrive as events. Postcondition: the profile points at the renewed certificate, or a failure reason is recorded. ### Acceptance Criteria - [ ] The renewal endpoint is published with its request and response DTOs and all error shapes - [ ] The three renewal resource events are defined - [ ] The `RENEW_SIGNING_PROFILE_CERTIFICATE` execution type is defined - [ ] Certificate validity status is available on signing profile list and detail DTOs - [ ] The `ResourceAction` the endpoint authorizes against is defined - [ ] OpenAPI regenerates cleanly - [ ] Sonar clean and coverage >= 80 %

title: mq-ai-hub.aioz.network intermittently serves an expired TLS certificate (expired Sep 2025) alongside a valid one
text: Environment: AIOZ DePIN CLI v1.2.6, Ubuntu 24.04.4, systemd service (freshly restarted before testing, ruling out client-side cert caching) Symptom: The consumer repeatedly fails to connect to amqps://mq-ai-hub.aioz.network:443, intermittently, with: [SSL: CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED] certificate verify failed: certificate has expired This occurs alongside successful connections within the same few-minute window, suggesting a load-balanced backend with inconsistent certificates. Root cause found: Repeated `openssl s_client -connect mq-ai-hub.aioz.network:443 -servername mq-ai-hub.aioz.network` calls, minutes apart, return two different leaf certificates for the same CN: - Valid: notBefore=Jun 13 2026, notAfter=Sep 11 2026 - Expired: notBefore=Jun 17 2025, notAfter=Sep 15 2025 (expired ~11 months as of this report) Both chain to a valid Let's Encrypt E6 intermediate (notAfter=Mar 12 2027), so the issue is isolated to the leaf cert on at least one backend node — it appears one server behind the LB/DNS pool never received the certificate renewal. Client-side ruled out: system clock NTP-synced and correct (timedatectl confirmed), latest CLI version, freshly restarted service, clean home connection (0% packet loss / ~7ms to 1.1.1.1). Impact: Intermittent failure to reach the AI task queue prevents reliable AI task assignment/consumption — ai_earned stays at zero in `reward balance` despite the AI worker processes running continuously.

author: christoph-maurer

title: Be alerted before a certificate expires
text: ## Story As a developer, I want to be told when a certificate is close to expiring, so that a renewal that has quietly stopped working is caught before visitors see a browser warning. ## Acceptance Criteria - [ ] Certificate expiry is checked from outside the server - [ ] An alert reaches somewhere actually read when expiry drops below ~20 days - [ ] The alert fires whatever the cause, including the certbot container not running at all - [ ] The check itself is verified once, by pointing it at a known-expired certificate ## Notes Split out of #48, where every other criterion was met and verified. This was the one left open, and it is the one guarding the failure mode that story cared about: renewal silently stopping and surfacing as an expired certificate 90 days later. Current state: renewal works and was tested end to end, both the certbot half and the nginx reload half. But a persistent failure is only visible in `docker compose logs certbot`, which depends on someone deciding to look. **Check from outside the box, not from inside it.** A hook in the certbot container cannot fire when the container is not running, which is one of the ways this fails. An external check on the live certificate catches every cause at once: expired, not renewed, not reloaded, container dead, server down. Twenty days is not arbitrary. Certbot renews at 30 days remaining and retries twice a day, so an alert at 20 means roughly 20 failed attempts have already happened and it is not a blip. Cheapest thing that works is an external uptime monitor with TLS expiry checking, several of which are free at this scale. Worth preferring to anything self-hosted here, since a monitor running on the same server cannot report that the server is down. Do not skip the last criterion. An alert that has never fired is not known to work, and this one stays silent for 70 days at a stretch. `expired.badssl.com` is a standing known-expired certificate suitable for testing against.
author: gislamog

title: Automate Zenoh server-certificate renewal and endpoint SAN management
text: ## Problem The generated Zenoh server certificate contains only a `localhost` SAN, expires after 365 days, and is generated only when certificate files are absent. Existing files are not validated or renewed before expiry. This conflicts with routable IPv4/IPv6/DNS endpoints and can cause a predictable device-ingress outage when the certificate reaches its first anniversary. ## Evidence - `crates/backend/src/domains/identity/cert_service.rs:125-158` - `crates/backend/src/init.rs:207-238,299-305` - `docs/deployment/openthread.md:81-112` ## Scope - Add configured DNS/IP SANs derived from explicitly advertised endpoints. - Validate issuer, SANs, key pair, and expiry during startup. - Renew before a configurable threshold. - Replace key/certificate files atomically. - Reload Zenoh TLS state safely or perform a controlled listener restart. - Export certificate expiry and last-rotation status. ## Acceptance criteria - [ ] Clients validate TLS through every configured advertised DNS/IP endpoint. - [ ] A near-expiry certificate renews before the configured threshold without plaintext fallback. - [ ] A healthy matching certificate is not needlessly regenerated. - [ ] Certificate replacement is atomic and cannot leave a mismatched key/certificate pair. - [ ] Expired, malformed, wrong-issuer, wrong-SAN, and near-expiry cases have automated tests. - [ ] Certificate expiry, renewal failures, and last successful rotation are visible in diagnostics and metrics. - [ ] A documented recovery path exists for failed rotation.

title: [Stability: Deadlines] ACME polling timeouts do not bound the HTTP operations they await
text: Severity: High Classification: Demonstrated deadline-enforcement gap. Location: /home/runner/work/BackFiller/BackFiller/src/BackFiller/Acme/AcmeOrderReadiness.cs:119–149 /home/runner/work/BackFiller/BackFiller/src/BackFiller/Acme/Protocol/AcmeClient.cs:200–230 /home/runner/work/BackFiller/BackFiller/src/BackFiller/Acme/Protocol/AcmeHttpTransport.cs:299–302 /home/runner/work/BackFiller/BackFiller/src/BackFiller/Acme/AcmeIssuer.cs:232–244 Code: C# var deadline = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow + timeout; OrderView? last = null; while (true) { cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested(); last = await pollAsync(cancellationToken).ConfigureAwait(false); The diagnostic failure path additionally performs: C# AcmeOrderResource resource = await acme.GetOrderAsync(order.Location, CancellationToken.None) .ConfigureAwait(false); Description: Deadlines are checked between polls, but the HTTP client has an infinite timeout and polls receive only caller cancellation. One stalled response can exceed the advertised readiness or finalization timeout indefinitely. The diagnostic request is worse: it can turn an already-failed issuance into an uncancellable wait. A stalled renewal prevents later renewal attempts and can ultimately leave the service with an expired certificate. Recommendation: Use linked deadline tokens for complete issuance phases and individual requests. Bound diagnostic requests independently. Use monotonic elapsed-time measurement for duration budgets. Validation: Exercise stalled headers, stalled bodies, and a stalled diagnostic request; verify each advertised deadline actually terminates its operation.

title: feat(webdav): investigate explicit trust for individual server certificates
text: ## Problem Self-hosted WebDAV servers may use certificates that the operating system does not trust. KeeForge currently uses system certificate validation and offers no explicit trust choice for an individual server certificate. This can prevent connecting to an otherwise intended self-hosted server. Certificate rejection is intentional current behavior. This request is a product design investigation for a new capability, rather than a blanket certificate-validation bypass. ## Proposed investigation - Design an explicit, opt-in trust decision scoped to the individual server origin and certificate. Keep normal system validation as the default and do not add a global “accept all certificates” switch. - Define what the confirmation UI displays: server hostname and port, certificate identity, issuer, validity dates, fingerprint, and the reason normal validation failed. Decide how a user can compare that information with a trusted source before confirming. - Distinguish self-signed or otherwise untrusted certificates from expired certificates, hostname mismatches, and TLS protocol/handshake failures. Decide which failures, if any, are eligible for an explicit exception and explain each clearly. - Define trust persistence, inspection, removal, and expiration. A certificate change must not silently inherit a prior exception; decide how reconfirmation works for legitimate renewal or server replacement, including interrupted/background operations. - Apply one consistent policy to connection setup, browsing, download, main-app cloud saves, and AutoFill-related cloud uploads. Define what happens when confirmation is required while the extension or a pending-upload drainer cannot present it, preserving unsaved/pending data until the main app can resolve the decision. - Preserve the existing same-origin redirect and credential protections; trust must not spread to another origin or unrelated provider. title: TLS interception dies when the proxy CA expires mid-session, with no way to recover without a restart
text: ### What happened? When the interception CA's `not_after` passes, a running proxy stops being able to serve intercepted TLS, and stays that way for the rest of the process's life: - Cached leaves are clamped to the CA's `not_after`, so they expire the moment it does — the client rejects them with `certificate has expired`. - A newly-seen SNI can't be minted at all: `mint_leaf` fails with `CA certificate has expired`, no chain is resolved, and rustls aborts the handshake. - The CA is only checked at startup, so nothing notices, and there's no path for a replacement CA to take effect in the running process. Every intercepted route is dead until the agent is restarted. The handshake WARN also blames the client (`Agent likely pins certs or carries a hard-coded trust list. Remove endpoint_rules / credential_key from the route…`) when the cause is our own expired CA, which sends people the wrong way. ### What did you expect to happen? That the session recovers on its own — a fresh CA takes effect in the running proxy without a restart. How that happens is open; the missing piece is that today there is no mechanism for it at all. ### Steps to reproduce 1. Save the profile below as `/tmp/ca-expiry/profile.json` — two intercepted routes, `ca_validity: "120s"`. 2. `nono proxy --profile /tmp/ca-expiry/profile.json --port 18080 --no-auth --verbose` — note the printed trust-bundle path. 3. `curl --proxy http://127.0.0.1:18080 --cacert https://example.com/` → 200, interception working, leaf cached. 4. Wait past 120s so the CA expires. 5. Re-request `https://example.com/` (cached leaf) → fails, expired certificate. 6. Request `https://example.net/`, not contacted before, so it forces a fresh mint → fails, no chain resolved. `ca_validity: "120s"` only compresses the timeline; the same thing happens to a long-lived trusted CA whenever a session outlives its certificate. ### Relevant output or logs ```shell $ openssl x509 -in -noout -dates # last cert in

title: Define registration expiry, a recovery period, and renewal after certificate lapse
text: We need to define what happens when a previously active registration's certificates expire and the customer does not renew them. Should the registration enter a recovery period, similar in purpose to domain redemption, before becoming terminal? Can the customer renew the same registration and version during that period, and what happens once it ends? Today, certificate expiry leaves the RA registration `ACTIVE`, even though the TL can show it as expired. The server-renewal route checks that stored state, so certificate lapse alone does not prevent a renewal request. Renewal also completes without a new TL event today. That is not a defined recovery policy. I lean toward a fixed recovery window rather than forcing a version bump as soon as a certificate expires: - The existing customer can recover the same registration and version during the window, after authenticating to the RA and providing fresh domain-control proof. Access to the old account, an old certificate, or a previous validation is not enough on its own. - The window preserves the option to recover the registration, not the validity of expired certificates. The registration must not be presented as usable again until the required certificates and DNS records are valid and the renewed state has been sealed in the TL. - Starting another renewal, retrying a failed request, or rotating a certificate without restoring the required set must not keep extending the recovery deadline. Recovery needs to complete before the deadline, with explicit rules for a request racing final retirement. - If recovery does not complete in time, the registration becomes terminal and its history remains intact. Under the current published-name rule, returning after that would mean a new registration with an unused version. We should explicitly agree whether that is the behavior we want. - Revocation is not certificate lapse. A revoked registration must not become recoverable through this path. title: The certificate will already be expired on the day the domain resolves again
text: ## Where The host: `/etc/letsencrypt/live/kada.click/`, the `kada-nginx` container. The DNS zone for `kada.click` (`dns23.hichina.com`, `dns24.hichina.com`, Aliyun). ## Problem The certificate expires **2026-10-13 01:53:31 UTC** and is being allowed to expire on purpose: the domain's A and AAAA records were removed for this host's ICP filing (备案), the site has no users while that is in progress, and the zone is not being touched for it. What makes this worth an issue rather than a note is the ordering. With no A records the name does not resolve at all, so an expired certificate is invisible to everyone - and the moment the filing ends and the records are restored, the site serves that certificate to the first visitor, with the browser warning that comes with it. Nothing in this repository observes the event that ends the deferral: `certbot.timer` runs every 12 hours and fails, while every check in `ci.yml` stays green (the on-host check passes `-k` deliberately, and the runner-side one is advisory). The renewal was attempted and cannot happen while the filing is in progress, which is recorded here so the search is not repeated: `standalone` cannot bind port 80 because `kada-nginx` holds it (`--network host`), and HTTP-01, webroot and TLS-ALPN-01 all fail while the name does not resolve (`no valid A records found for kada.click`; NXDOMAIN for `www.kada.click`). DNS-01 is the only authenticator that works, and because it validates through a TXT record it can be run **before** the records are restored - which is what makes the first item below possible at all. ## Done when - The certificate is renewed **before** the A/AAAA records are restored, so no visitor ever meets the expired one. - The renewal is done from two SSH sessions, because `dig` has to run while certbot waits on `Press Enter to Continue` - adding the records in the same session is what failed the first attempt: ```bash # session A sudo certbot certonly --manual --preferred-challenges dn

title: [Post-Incident] INC-2024-007: bookshop-srv: HTTPS handshake failures — TLS certificate expired on ingress
text: ## Post-Incident Report — INC-2024-007 > **Severity:** P1 | **Service:** `bookshop-srv` | **Time:** 2024-04-28T03:15:42Z > **Category:** Infrastructure (tls_certificate) > **Known pattern:** This matches a previously resolved incident (INC-2024-018). Resolution was accelerated using the knowledge base. --- ### Incident Timeline ```mermaid timeline title INC-2024-007 Incident Timeline section Trigger 03:00 : Infrastructure event detected : Category - tls_certificate section Detection 03:15 : Metrics anomaly detected : 100% error rate 03:17 : Alert fired - P1 section Response 03:19 : AIOps Agent diagnosed root cause : Confidence - high 03:21 : Remediation PR + workflow dispatched ``` --- ### Impact All HTTPS traffic to bookshop.example.com — 100% HTTPS handshake failures. **Affected endpoints:** ingress-nginx, cert-manager, bookshop-tls certificate ### Root Cause Cert-manager's HTTP-01 solver for Let's Encrypt ACME challenges was not correctly routed through the ingress. As a result, the ACME server could not verify the challenge URL during renewal, leading to repeated failure and eventual certificate expiry. **Category:** Infrastructure incident — No blame PR. Root cause is an infrastructure issue: misconfigured cert-manager HTTP-01 solver ingress route, preventing certificate renewal. **Confidence:** high ### Immediate Actions - [ ] Fix the ingress configuration for the cert-manager HTTP-01 solver route to ensure Let's Encrypt ACME challenge requests can succeed. - [ ] Manually trigger a certificate renewal by deleting and recreating the Certificate resource. - [ ] Temporarily patch the affected ingress to serve traffic over HTTP for critical business continuity, if downtime cannot be tolerated. ### Remediation Update the cert-manager HTTP-01 solver ingress resource to correctly route /.well-known/acme-challenge/ paths

title: Loki's TLS certificate has expired, so an unflagged curl returns empty and reads as a healthy fleet
text: ⚠️ **Measured 2026-08-18 19:49 CT while reading the CTL-879 instrument.** ``` $ curl -sS -G "https://loki.otel.rozich.com/loki/api/v1/query_range" ... curl: (60) SSL certificate problem: certificate has expired ``` The same request with `-k` returns **HTTP 200** and correct data, so Loki itself is healthy — only the certificate is expired. ## Why this matters more than it looks Loki is the fleet's primary read surface for daemon logs. `AGENTS.md` → "Working the Loop" makes the observability read the **first** move for diagnosing a wedge, and the `sensing-substrate` skill's whole cookbook is LogQL against this endpoint. ⛔ **The failure mode is a silent false-clean.** Any agent or script that runs `curl` without `-k` and does not check the exit code gets **empty output**, which reads exactly like "no matching log lines" — i.e. like a healthy fleet. That is the mechanism `AGENTS.md` names as trap (1)/(5) in "Reporting a negative → run a positive control first". A lane could report "no `ctl-879` lines, the board is fine" purely because the TLS handshake failed. ## Acceptance criteria * **Given** `https://loki.otel.rozich.com`, **when** a client performs default certificate verification, **then** the handshake succeeds (no `-k` needed). * **Given** the fix, **then** the same check is applied to the sibling endpoints on that host (Grafana, Prometheus, Tempo) — a single expiring cert is rarely alone. * **Given** renewal, **then** there is an alert or automated renewal so the next expiry is not discovered by a lane mid-incident. ## Notes * Found while reading the CTL-2033 instrument for CTL-879 / CTL-2039. I read through it with `-k` explicitly and said so on the channel rather than reporting the query as impossible or reporting an empty result. * The stack lives in the sister repo `catalyst-otel`; the fix may belong there rather than here.

title: links: daily check red since 2026-09-06 -- code.bioconductor.org TLS cert expired (footer link, 44/46 errors)
text: ## What broke The `links` workflow went red on 2026-09-06 (run 34031006128): 46 errors, lychee exit 2. Previous day was green. ## Diagnosis **44 of 46 errors are one URL**: `https://code.bioconductor.org/` — the "Browsable Code Base" link in `astro/src/components/Footer.astro`, so it appears on every checked page. ``` failed to verify TLS certificate: invalid peer certificate: certificate expired: certificate is not valid after 1788103116 ``` Confirmed from outside CI: ``` $ openssl s_client -connect code.bioconductor.org:443 | openssl x509 -noout -dates -issuer notBefore=Jul 29 15:18:36 2025 GMT notAfter=Aug 30 15:18:36 2026 GMT issuer=... Go Daddy Secure Certificate Authority - G2 ``` The cert expired **2026-08-30**. The check stayed green for a week because the last successful result was inside lychee's 14-day cache window; the cache entry aged out today and the fresh check hit the expired cert. This is upstream Bioconductor infrastructure, not anything in this repo. Needs a cert renewal by whoever runs code.bioconductor.org. ## The other 2 - `https://us06web.zoom.us/meeting/register/qtozL2LDSkK2-7eXxFdlVw` → 404, on `/developers/how-to/c-debugging/`. Genuine rot in imported legacy prose (not in git source; comes from the data snapshot). Belongs in the #23 ledger. - `http://www.gnu.org/software/gdb/` → timeout, on `/developers/how-to/mavericks-howto/`. Returns 200 now; transient. ## Decision (2026-09-06) No change to `astro/.lycheeignore`. The badge stays red until code.bioconductor.org renews its cert. If it is still expired in a day or two, file an issue with Bioconductor core (the owners of code.bioconductor.org). The zoom 404 on `/developers/how-to/c-debugging/` is genuine inherited rot and can go into the #23 ledger whenever that file is next touched.

title: Drupal connector: collect and push TLS evidence without Sentinel inbound access
text: ## Outcome Let the site report certificate evidence through its existing authenticated outbound push. The Drupal request alone does not reveal a CDN or reverse-proxy certificate. ## Scope - [ ] Discover the hosting TLS termination model and support explicit collectors: configured local TLS endpoint, public certificate metadata from a host/provider collector, or separately enabled site-originated public TLS check. - [ ] A self-check to the public hostname is still an external connection from the site; require explicit configuration and never enable it as a hidden fallback. - [ ] Record hostname, source (origin/edge/local), observed time, validity dates, issuer/fingerprint and actual validation coverage. Do not send private keys or arbitrary file contents. - [ ] Keep permissions, timeout, cron throttle and evidence cadence explicit; bounded authenticated certificate heartbeat must survive unchanged inventory. - [ ] Do not call the certificate used for the Sentinel API connection the customer website certificate. - [ ] Restrict collectors to administrator-configured targets; bound DNS resolution/connect/handshake time and destination changes. Do not accept arbitrary payload-driven URLs or file paths. Local targets need an explicit hosting configuration. - [ ] Keep inventory submission usable when TLS collection fails; send a distinct failed/unavailable observation. Record measurement location and split-DNS limitations. ## Acceptance and verification - [ ] Fixtures cover local termination, CDN with different edge/origin certificates, unavailable evidence, renewal and expired certificate. - [ ] No Sentinel-to-site inbound request is needed; disabled collectors make no self-connection. - [ ] Settings/logs explain what was checked and what remains unknown; existing push compatibility and secret handling remain intact. ## Dependencies Sentinel companion TLS ingestion/policy issue; current certificate feature truecms/sentinel#396. PHP options: https://www.php.net/man

title: HTTPS certificate hot-reload never sees a certbot or Kubernetes Secret renewal (the watched path is resolved once at start)
text: ## Context The HTTPS certificate hot-reload (`CertReloader`, on by default, polling every `--cert-reload-interval`, 60 s) resolves the `--https-cert` and `--https-key` paths with `std::filesystem::canonical` once, in its constructor, and from then on polls the modification time of the files they resolved to. A rotation that replaces a symlink instead of rewriting the file is therefore never seen: the file the watcher resolved at start is either unchanged or gone, and `files_changed()` returns false in both cases. The server keeps serving the old certificate until it is restarted. Both common layouts are affected. The certbot recipe in `docs/operations/certificate-renewal.md` points `--https-cert` at `/etc/letsencrypt/live/ /fullchain.pem`, a symlink into `archive/`; a certificate mounted from a Kubernetes Secret is a symlink chain through the kubelet's `..data` link, whose target directory is replaced on every update. With the 90-day certbot lifetime this ends in a served-expired-certificate outage unless someone restarts the server after the first renewal. It is a reliability gap in a documented configuration, not a data exposure. ## Evidence - `server/core/src/cert_reloader.cpp:58-64`: the constructor canonicalises `cert_path` and `key_path` once and records their mtimes (`:68`, `:73`). - `:123-133`: `files_changed()` compares the mtimes of those canonical paths and returns false when `last_write_time` fails ("file temporarily missing during atomic rename -- skip"). - Emulation of exactly those two calls (a throwaway program outside the repo, same `canonical` and `last_write_time` on a temporary tree): - certbot-style rotation (`live/server.pem` repointed from `archive/server1.pem` to `archive/server2.pem`): the canonical path is still `server1.pem`, its mtime is unchanged, `files_changed()` is false; reading the configured path now yields the new certificate. - Kubernetes-style rotation (`..data` repointed to a new directory, old directory removed
author: Doomgoose

title: Node: an expired stored certificate retries renewal for ever without saying the certificate expired
text: \`install_identity\` (crates/roxy-node/src/node.rs ~306) computes \`left = 0\` for an expired certificate so renewal fires at once, but the control plane rejects the handshake and the result surfaces as \`CertificateError::Failed\` / \`LeaseFetch::Failed\`, a "lease fetch failed" warning every poll. Fail-closed and as documented, but the operator never reads "certificate expired" and the fix (new token, empty state dir) is not suggested. Fix: log \`not_after < now\` once at startup and on each renewal attempt, naming the re-enrolment steps. Found reviewing at 8adb52f.

text: ### To Reproduce 1. Install Dokploy at a release pinning an older Traefik (e.g. v0.29.13 → `3.6.7`). 2. Upgrade Dokploy to v0.30.2 (pins `3.6.25`). 3. `docker exec dokploy-traefik traefik version` 4. Observe the old version still running. ### Current vs. Expected behavior ## Expected behavior After upgrading Dokploy to v0.30.2, `dokploy-traefik` runs `traefik:v3.6.25`. ## Actual behavior `dokploy-traefik` continued running **`traefik:v3.6.7`** ### Provide environment information ```bash - Dokploy updated from **v0.29.13 → v0.30.2** - Docker on Linux ``` ### Which area(s) are affected? (Select all that apply) Traefik, Installation ### Are you deploying the applications where Dokploy is installed or on a remote server? Same server where Dokploy is installed ### Additional context ## Impact 1. Traefik upstream security patches never land in production. 2. Traefik bundles lego, so a stale Traefik means stale ACME code. 3. An already fixed Traefik Docker Engine incompatibility can resurface anytime #4324 #4123 ### Example to what Nr.2 can lead In my case the running Traefik (v3.6.1, meaning the container had already been stale for several upgrades before this one) carried a lego version whose Infomaniak DNS provider could not parse the provider's API response (`json: cannot unmarshal number into Go struct field APIResponse[string].data of type string`, fixed upstream in lego v5.2.0 via go-acme/lego#3139, vendored into Traefik from 3.6.22 onward). title: SMTP notification failure marks successful certificate renewal as failed
text: ## Description When SMTP is configured but unavailable or authentication fails, KCert can successfully complete an ACME renewal and save the new certificate to the Kubernetes TLS secret. After saving the certificate, KCert attempts to send a notification email. If sending that notification fails, the SMTP exception propagates into the renewal workflow. KCert then reports the already completed renewal as an unexpected renewal failure and increments the renewal service failure counter. Notification delivery is secondary functionality and should not change the result of a successful certificate renewal. ## Environment * KCert image: `nabsul/kcert:v1.2.0` * Kubernetes Ingress * ACME provider: Let's Encrypt production * SMTP provider: Microsoft 365 * SMTP authentication unavailable or invalid ## Steps to reproduce 1. Configure KCert with working ACME settings. 2. Configure SMTP with credentials that cannot authenticate, or make the SMTP service unavailable. 3. Trigger the creation or renewal of a managed certificate. 4. Allow the ACME order to complete. 5. Inspect the KCert logs and the resulting Kubernetes TLS secret. ## Actual behaviour The ACME order completes successfully: ```text Finalize ...: valid Finalized order and received cert URI: ... Saved cert ``` The Kubernetes TLS secret contains the newly issued certificate, and ingress-nginx serves that new certificate. KCert then attempts to send the renewal notification. When SMTP authentication fails, it logs: ```text Unexpected renewal failure System.Net.Mail.SmtpException: 535 5.7.3 Authentication unsuccessful ``` The stack trace shows the exception propagating through: ```text KCert.Services.EmailClient.SendAsync KCert.Services.EmailClient.NotifyRenewalResultAsync KCert.Services.KCertClient.RenewCertAsync ``` The renewal service then counts this SMTP notification failure as a service failure: ```text Renewal Service encountered error 1 of max 5 ``` After another successful certificate renewal fol

title: CLEAR VENTURE v282.0.0
text: ## 🚨 Production incident — emergency investigation **Affected website:** https://lacuisinederosalie.ca **Reported:** 2026-10-15 (Eastern Time) **Severity:** Critical / production website inaccessible **Area:** Engineering / hosting / TLS / domain configuration ### Situation The client-facing production site has suddenly become entirely inaccessible, despite **GitHub deployments appearing to complete successfully**. The browser blocks entry on the domain because HTTPS certificate validation fails. The website uses HSTS, so visitors cannot proceed past the browser warning. ### Exact browser error ```text Your connection is not private Attackers might be trying to steal your information from lacuisinederosalie.ca net::ERR_CERT_DATE_INVALID lacuisinederosalie.ca normally uses encryption to protect your information. When Chrome tried to connect to lacuisinederosalie.ca this time, the website sent back unusual and incorrect credentials. You cannot visit lacuisinederosalie.ca right now because the website uses HSTS. ``` ### Required investigation (immediate) 1. **Confirm outage and capture TLS evidence** for the apex domain and `www` (if configured): served certificate subject/SAN, issuer, `notBefore`/`notAfter`, full chain, which endpoint serves it, DNS resolutions and HTTPS responses from more than one network. Determine whether the certificate expired, is not yet valid, or there is a local-clock/chain issue. 2. **Inspect DNS and hosting ownership**: registrar/nameservers, A/AAAA/CNAME records, GitHub Pages custom domain configuration, and any Cloudflare proxy/Pages/Worker or other edge endpoint in front of the site. Verify the domain is routed to the intended deployment and not to stale infrastructure. 3. **Trace TLS provisioning/renewal**: identify who issues and renews the visitor-facing certificate (GitHub Pages, Cloudflare or another provider); inspect failed validation, ACME challenges, CAA records, certificate/SSL status and relevant provider events. title: Complete cross-platform networking and trusted portless HTTPS, including Windows
text: ## Problem Porto already provides stable local HTTP routes, a local CA, TLS/SNI certificates, Kubernetes Gateway-based service routing, and a trusted portless HTTPS helper on macOS. The remaining gap is consistent host integration: first-class direct container/VM connectivity, proxy/VPN-aware behavior, and trusted portless HTTPS on Windows and Linux. At [b605be8](https://github.com/mbianchidev/porto/tree/b605be821cf8c08434a83ec98aedae30f17771ff), `docs/networking.md` documents the macOS helper and nonstandard fallback ports. Relevant code includes `internal/localhttps/`, `internal/certificates/`, `internal/docker/`, and the existing Kubernetes gateway/forwarding managers. The closed certificate foundation #6 does not track this cross-platform implementation. ## Requested implementation - Extend the existing `porto https install/status/uninstall` experience and dashboard controls to Windows and Linux using appropriate least-privilege OS integrations; do not replace the working macOS path. - On Windows, provide loopback-only portless HTTPS, native certificate-store trust, renewable certificates, and an installed helper/service or equivalent transport with a clear ownership/lifecycle model. Request elevation only for actions that actually require it; do not run the daemon or workloads as administrator. - Make first-use trust, renewal, browser trust limitations, port conflicts, repair, and uninstall understandable. Preserve unrelated certificates, services, firewall rules, and listeners; never fix TLS by disabling certificate validation. - Provide convenient container and managed-VM addresses/hostnames and a documented direct-IP reachability capability for supported backends. Do not silently expose workloads to the LAN or change unrelated routes. - Integrate system or explicitly configured HTTP/HTTPS/SOCKS proxies, bypass rules, and trusted registry CAs where supported. Store proxy credentials securely and redact diagnostics. - Handle VPN/split-DNS changes, subnet c

This is clearly mentioned in the plugin description. We have written FREE PLUGIN FEATURES vs PREMIUM PLUGIN FEATURES transparently there. We announced the pro version on November 3, 2020, and explained the difficulties of spending hundreds of hours developing the plugin and then spending time providing support without any monetary return . Since then for 1 year and 8 months, we notified our users with admin notice with a link to this blog post: https://freessl.tech/blog/auto-install-free-ssl-needs-your-help-to-survive/ . So, if you are a previous user, you can still use the plugin at no cost till December 31, 2022. The benefits of the Free version are that users still get Let’s Encrypt™ SSL Certificate is FREE. But they provide it through their API. If you are not a programmer, you need to study and practice programming for years to be able to use the API of Let’s Encrypt™ to generate a single Free SSL Certificate for your WordPress website. Here is where ‘Auto-Install Free SSL’ comes into play. With this WordPress plugin, you can generate the Let’s Encrypt™ Free SSL Certificate with ease! You don’t need to have programming or coding experience to set it up. However, you need to spend some time using this tool to generate & install the SSL certificate and repeat this for every renewal (every 2-3 months). The premium version does this for you automatically and saves users’ time. And time is money for many people . Now it’s the users’ choice which version they use. Regarding the pricing of SSL certificates, many popular web hosting companies charge $100 or more for 1 year SSL certificate. We know, users used to purchase products they found cheaper. codewarrior78 (@codewarrior78) 3 years, 12 months ago You can get cheap ssl certificates for a lot less then $10!. text: Doesn’t even redirect… - [Really Simple Security - Simple and Performant Security (formerly Really Simple SSL)] Review | WordPress.org Skip to content Showcase Plugins Themes Hosting News Resources Learn WordPress Documentation Education Forums Developers Blocks Patterns Photos Openverse ↗ ︎ WordPress.tv ↗ ︎ About About WordPress Make WordPress Events Five for the Future Enterprise Gutenberg ↗ ︎ Job Board ↗ ︎ Swag ↗ ︎ Get WordPress Search in WordPress.org Get WordPress Forums Welcome to Support Guidelines Get involved Log in Welcome to Support Guidelines Get involved Log in Skip to content Forums / Plugin: Really Simple Security - Simple and Performant Security (formerly Really Simple SSL) / Doesn’t even redirect… Search for: Search forums Doesn’t even redirect… andywest (@andywest) 1 year, 3 months ago I installed this solely for the 301 redirection, and it doesn’t even do it… and to top it off, it left my site in maintenance mode, so had to FTP in and delete the plugin… Why does it need all the bloatware Viewing 1 replies (of 1 total) Plugin Support jarnovos (@jarnovos) 1 year, 3 months ago Hi @andywest , Sorry to hear about the issue you experienced. WordPress itself automatically activates Maintenance Mode when updating plugins/themes and such; but if the update process is interrupted (e.g., due to a slow server, internet disconnection or similar), the .maintenance file might not be removed from the root folder of your WordPress site (same folder as the wp-config.php file) causing Maintenance Mode to persist. If you manually remove that file, Maintenance Mode will be disabled. The 301 redirect to HTTPS has always been one of the core features of this plugin since it’s release, and should of course work without any such issues. If you need any assistance with setting it up, feel free to open a thread on the Support Forums of this plugin ( https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/really-simple-ssl/ ) as we would be more than happy to take a look at the issue.
